rv.q: After the Act is light years away from depressing – although it is salutary to recall that Section 28 was only repealed in 2003.
For all its exuberant defiance, After the Act is a serious and timely reminder of that fact.
The songs are super fun, but the prose-to-music sections can be dense and complicated, and with the multi-layered music, some passages are barely penetrable.
Welcome to the worst show of the year so far... so inept that part of me suspects it must be part of some Reform UK psy-ops campaign to put political theatre out of business.
The result is confrontational, painfully timely, and if you will excuse the theatre criticism cliche, essential viewing.
After the Act bubbles with life while still being serious, both angry and funny, and hey!
If this production were too polished or too glitzy, it would somehow work against its representation of a grassroots movement.
After the Act is a wonderful piece of documentary theatre that had a critically acclaimed national run before coming to the Royal Court Theatre.
After The Act is a soul-crushing but ultimately uplifting musical that balances the light with the serious and moves just as much as it entertains.
It is a celebratory piece of theatre that always engages and cleverly weaves together personal stories of hurt, rebellion, and also joy.
It is an important piece, well-researched and pertinent to today.
Silenced voices struggle to be heard in this moving but messy show.

cn.t: This verbatim musical about Section 28's impact on the LGBTQ+ community earns praise for its timely, heartfelt subject matter and empowering spirit, though critics split on execution—some find it fizzing and moving, others messy and chaotic.
